The Plugins line counts the installed plugins; with none it points to oc-plugin search. The prompt is coloured and shows the folder you're in. It works in the printer's own shell, so nothing extra needs installing. If bash is installed through Entware, the login uses bash instead.

  • Only interactive logins get it. SFTP, scp and ssh <printer> <command> aren't affected, so scripts and file transfers work as before.
  • The logo needs a UTF-8 terminal. Windows Terminal, PuTTY and the macOS and Linux terminals all use UTF-8 by default.
  • With bash, your own ~/.bashrc can still set a different prompt.
  • Rolling back to stock removes it. It also turns itself off if FlashForge's firmware is put back any other way, such as a FlashForge update.

To turn it off on your printer, delete /etc/profile.d/opencreator.sh and /usr/data/opencreator/startup/scripts/03-login.sh.

items.title: Safety features
items.text:
• Model check

    Only a Creator 5 (PID 0028) or Creator 5 Pro (PID 0029) on a supported kernel package is accepted. Otherwise installing is blocked.

  • Backup first

    Before anything changes, FlashForge's firmwareExe, Moonraker, the opencreator folder (Klipper and your config), the web UI folders and the nginx config are archived to the USB drive.

  • Restore

    If a backup exists, the installer offers Restore backup, also right after a failed install. Folders that did not exist before are removed again. MCU firmware is not rolled back, and Entware stays installed.

  • Preflight warnings

    Warns when there is less than 256 MB free on the printer or the USB drive, or the backup folder is missing or read-only.

  • Log

    The Log button shows everything the installer did. The same log is saved to the USB drive as opencreator-installer.log.

  • Demo install

    Runs every step for real, but writes into a separate folder instead of the system, so you can see exactly what would change without touching the printer.

When the install finishes, it records what was installed (installer version, model, mode, web UI, touchscreen, backup location and time) in /usr/data/opencreator/install.json. The next run shows that as the previous install.

Power

Do not power off the printer while the installer is running, especially during MCU flashing. A power loss there can leave the printer needing firmware recovery.

items.title: Is OpenCreator CFW for you?
items.text: OpenCreator CFW replaces FlashForge's software on the Creator 5 and Creator 5 Pro with Kalico, Moonraker and a web UI. It's in public alpha, so it suits some people more than others.

items.title: You'll like CFW if you
items.text:
• Want faster toolchanges

    Up to 2x faster: about 6 seconds on stock, as little as 3 seconds on CFW.

  • Want a full web UI

    Fluidd or Mainsail with Moonraker, straight from the mainstream projects. You don't need the touchscreen at all.

  • Like to tune and tinker

    Kalico with MPC, corrected PID, input shaper graphs on the printer, per-tool Z offsets, toggles for purge, flow calibration, bed soak and more. See CFW Features.

  • Use OrcaSlicer

    Print over the Moonraker agent, with material and colour synced from every tool like an AMS.

  • Want FlashForge's services gone

    You can disable them completely, cloud included.

  • Want to run a Raspberry Pi as host

    Move Klipper onto an SBC for more power and cameras. See OpenCreator for SBC.

  • Want better prints and camera quality

    With features like better VFA compensation you can get cleaner prints, and with camera tweaks, you can have the best looking camera.

  • Want a quieter printer

    We adaptively scale fan noise to what your temperature actually is, making it quiet when it's cold, and loud when its hot.

  • Want AI detection

    With our special hand-crafted model in collaboration with Printer Buddy, we give you Printer Buddy Lite The best available local AI vision model for your Creator 5, running as a plugin to addon, with zero performance overhead.

  • Want an ever growing plugin list

    With a small command or two, you can download addons instantly compatible and available for your printer.

  • Want a printer that's hard to brick

    On stock, a broken startup script means opening the printer to recover it. CFW boots even then, and a recovery script on a USB stick fixes it from outside. See Early boot and recovery stick.

  • Want what's coming next

    More is on the way, including more accurate pressure advance tuned to your filament, and stall and skipped step detection (StallGuard-like) on X, Y and Z, to even better VFA testing and compensation.

items.title: CFW may not be for you yet if you
items.text:
• Rely on the stock touchscreen. GrumpyScreen replaces it fully, new UI.
  • Use FlashForge's app, cloud or FlashStudio. These go away once FlashForge's services are gone.
  • Care about your warranty. Installing mods may void it. You can clean up any traces but they still may figure it out.
  • Want official support. You can't ask FlashForge for software support if you're on custom firmware.
  • Have zero prior experience with 3D printing. You're expected to have at least a basic understanding of Klipper. We can help, but we aren't perfect.
  • Your main language is anything other than English. Currently, multi-lingual support is basic and not automatic. In development!

items.title: Not sure?
items.text: OpenCreator Legacy keeps the mostly stock FlashForge experience, with creature comforts like better camera views. If CFW sounds right, head to Getting started, and ask in the Discord if you have questions.

items.title: MCU development and verification
items.text:
OpenCreator has separate host software, printer configuration, and firmware for four controller boards. They should be fully working as of 19 of October.

Board MCU Primary role MainboardGD GD32H737VGT6 Main motion and machine I/O eBoard N32G455CCL7 Shared extrusion drive and pressure-advance sensing Heaterboard N32G455REL7 Tool heaters and temperature I/O Levelboard N32G430F8S7 Probing and levelboard sensing

The source for the MCU ports and the host is in kalico. It replaces klipper-c5, which is archived and kept for reference only. The configuration is maintained separately in opencreator-fs and opencreator-tunnel.

items.title: One motor, four logical tools
items.text:
T0 through T3 represent four removable toolheads, but they share one physical extruder motor and its eBoard TMC2209 driver. The logical extruders share the eBoard step, direction, and enable signals. Tool selection associates that drive with the selected heater, sensors, and filament state; it does not switch among four independent motor drivers.

The printer and tunneled configurations have a [tmc2209 extruder] through [tmc2209 extruder3] section, all with identical settings and all addressing the same driver. Each logical extruder needs one so that it requests the same step-on-both-edges (DEDGE) mode as the others. A tool without one sends single-edge pulses, and the driver, already in DEDGE mode, counts each pulse twice, so that tool extrudes about double. Their configured pins are eBoard PB11 for UART receive, PB10 for UART transmit, address 0, PB14 for step, PB15 for direction, and PB12 for enable. The eBoard uses USART3 for this driver. The host's Creator 5 UART transport and the eBoard's MCU command must both be present; ordinary GPIO UART bitbanging does not implement this hardware path. The configured 0.70 A current approximates stock behavior. The assumed 0.110-ohm sense resistor has been verified working.

Each logical extruder is a separate MCU stepper on the same PB15 direction pin. Stock Klipper toggles a stepper's direction pin relative to that stepper's own last direction, so with four steppers on one pin the actual level ends up as the XOR of all four. A tool then runs backwards whenever an odd number of the other tools last moved in reverse, for example a retract before docking. eBoard builds (CONFIG_C5_EBOARD) therefore write the absolute direction at the start of every move in src/stepper.c. This needs the eBoard reflashed; until then a FIRMWARE_RESTART resets all four to forward.

items.title: Shared MCUs across older printers
items.text:
The MCUs are heavily shared.

Older printers such as the AD5X and AD5M both have the same Nations MCU, but the Gigadevice GD32 chip for the main MCU is completely new, and has not been seen on any other 3D printer made yet. A lot of libraries such as MCLib and addons such as VFA testing are assumed or said to be made by GigaDevice, the MCU manufacturer. In the grape vine, there is supposed to be another printer coming out with the same MCU but as a revision, not a new release.

How MCLib drives the motors, and how Kalico's replacement for it works, is documented in Architecture.

items.title: Quieter motors
items.text:
Testing

This is in testing on the Kalico phase-stepping branch and needs its mainboard firmware. It isn't in a release yet.

The Creator 5's mainboard drives the X, Y and Z motors itself, through FlashForge's MCLib motor control (see VFA compensation). OpenCreator changes two things in it to make the motors quieter, mostly at printing speeds up to about 100 mm/s:

  • Step interpolation follows the real move between steps.
  • Ripple correction cancels the motors' own wobble, calibrated per motor with the toolhead accelerometer.

items.title: Step interpolation
items.text:
Klipper sends the mainboard a step for each 1/16 of a full step. Between steps the mainboard moves the motor smoothly on to the next one, about 20,000 times a second. Stock guesses when the next step comes by assuming it takes as long as the last one. That is right at a steady speed but wrong whenever the speed changes, so the motor runs ahead or falls behind and then snaps back on the next step. Speed changes are constant in a print: acceleration, input shaping and pressure advance all change it.

On OpenCreator the mainboard's step queue already knows exactly when the next step is due, so the motor is moved on at the real rate. After the last step of a move it stays on that step, instead of running nearly a step past it like stock does.

Nothing changes on the Klipper side: homing, endstops and positions work as before.

items.title: Ripple correction
items.text:
A stepper motor doesn't turn perfectly evenly. Its detent torque and the shape of its current give it a small wobble at fixed multiples of its electrical cycle (four full steps). On the Creator 5 the strong ones are 2, 4, 6 and 8 times per cycle; 4 is once per full step. The wobble shakes the toolhead at those frequencies, so it moves with speed: at 10 mm/s the once-per-step wobble is at 49 Hz, at 20 mm/s at 99 Hz. That is most of the hum you hear at printing speeds.

Ripple correction adds a small opposite current to each motor at those multiples, timed to the motor's position. The right current depends on the speed: for the once-per-step wobble it shrinks as the speed nears the motor's resonance, flips over, and grows again above it. So each multiple has a table of corrections at five speeds, and the mainboard picks the value for the current speed from the step rate. Just above the fastest and below the slowest calibrated speed the correction fades out, as nothing was measured there.

It is calibrated per motor, and per direction of travel, with the toolhead accelerometer.

items.title: Calibrating
items.text:
Dock all the toolheads, then send:

RIPPLE_CALIBRATE

It homes, picks up the first tool and parks in the middle. Then, for each motor, it moves along the diagonal that turns only that motor and measures the vibration at each multiple. It takes about 10 minutes a motor and ends with SAVE_CONFIG. Add AXIS=X or AXIS=Y to do one motor, or SAVE=0 to leave saving for later.

Each speed it tries prints the vibration before and after:

stepper_x harmonic 4 at 297 Hz (60 mm/s motor): forward 565 -> 33, reverse 567 -> 13 mm/s^2

Run it again after changing motors or belts.

items.title: How it finds the correction
items.text:
At one speed, the vibration's strength at a multiple is a simple curve (a quadratic) in the correction's size and timing. Measuring it with no change and with three small test corrections fixes that curve, and the best correction is at its bottom. One more move checks it, and it is only kept if the vibration went down. It does this twice, the second time with smaller test corrections. Both directions are measured on the same out-and-back move.

MCLIB_RIPPLE_MEASURE STEPPER=stepper_x SPEED=30 shows the vibration at each multiple at one speed, and MCLIB_SET_RIPPLE STEPPER=stepper_x shows the saved tables.

items.title: With VFA compensation
items.text: VFA compensation also corrects the 1, 2 and 4 times ripples, but tuned near the frame's resonance, so mostly at higher speeds. The mainboard hands over by speed: where a ripple table covers the motor's current speed, it replaces the VFA value for that ripple; outside the table VFA takes over again, blended in between. Keep both calibrated.

items.title: Fans during calibration
items.text: Calibration holds the mainboard and power supply fans at 50% and waits for them to settle before measuring, like input shaper and VFA calibration do. Otherwise they speed up as the mainboard warms during the test, and their changing vibration throws the measurements off.

items.title: Measured
items.text:
Creator 5 Pro, toolhead accelerometer, board fans held at 50% throughout. The new firmware (step interpolation plus calibrated ripple correction) is the average of three sessions, against the firmware before these changes. Numbers are how much less the toolhead shakes, in three frequency bands: 10–100 / 100–300 / 300–800 Hz. "Diagonal" moves one motor only.

Move Change Y 5 mm/s −24% / −39% / −58% Y 10 mm/s −37% / −38% / −52% Y 20 mm/s −42% / −54% / −45% Y 80 mm/s −4% / −30% / +1% X 5 mm/s −40% / −15% / −17% X 10 mm/s −34% / +18% / −4% X 20 mm/s −23% / −42% / −36% X 40 mm/s +2% / −27% / −4% X 80 mm/s −12% / −22% / −9% X 150 mm/s −11% / −6% / −4% Diagonal 5 mm/s −34% / −29% / −16% Diagonal 20 mm/s −32% / −62% / −14% Diagonal 80 mm/s +2% / −14% / −13% Slow speed changes −2 to −17% / −6 to −10% / −5 to −14%

Repeating the same test 15 minutes apart moves single numbers by up to about ±30%, so read small changes as no change. At the speed each point was calibrated at, the wobble it targets drops by 75 to 95%. The rest of the vibration is the frame and belts, which this doesn't touch; input shaping handles that.

items.title: Inspiration: Prusa's phase stepping
items.text:
This work builds on what Prusa Research published about phase stepping on the Original Prusa XL (firmware 6.0) and later the CORE One. They showed that every stepper motor turns slightly unevenly in its own way, which causes both noise and vertical fine artifacts, and that correcting each motor's drive signal, calibrated by moving the head diagonally at several speeds while recording the toolhead accelerometer, removes most of it. Prusa reported over 96% less motor vibration on the XL. Their help article covers the calibration.

What we took from it: per-motor correction of the motor's own ripple, calibrated with the accelerometer on moves that turn one motor at a time, at several speeds. No Prusa code is used. What differs on the Creator 5:

Prusa phase stepping OpenCreator Motor driver Trinamic stepper drivers The mainboard's own motor control (MCLib), adding a correcting current Steps Replaced: the firmware drives the motor phases from the motion plan (hence the name) Kept: Klipper still sends steps, the mainboard follows the real move between them Correction Per motor and direction Per motor and direction, with a table of corrections per speed Crash detection Turned off while it's on Not affected (skipped step detection is the separate, optional motion guard)

items.title: Why not full phase stepping
items.text: Prusa's phase stepping has the printer's computer send the motor's exact path instead of steps. Step interpolation already follows the path to within a fraction of a 1/16 step, and the measurements show the remaining noise is the motors' wobble, not step size. So OpenCreator does the part that removes it, the ripple correction, without changing how Klipper talks to the mainboard.

items.title: OpenCreator CFW
items.text:
OpenCreator full custom firmware, or CFW, is the deeper Creator 5 integration effort. It aims to make the printer's host software, MCU behavior, toolchanging, and configuration maintainable as one community-developed stack. The goal is more features and more stable software overall compared to stock. CFW is in public alpha; get the latest release. The mostly stock alternative is OpenCreator Legacy.

The work is split between kalico for Klipper and MCU integration (it replaces klipper-c5, which is archived), and opencreator-fs for printer files, configuration, and installation helpers.

items.title: What the newer path aims to support
items.text:
Full custom firmware area Goal Status Base software Maintain Creator 5 stock behavior in a community-developed Klipper host and MCU stack. Finished Installation and updates Provide a tested CFW installation. Finished Tool selection Configure T0 to T3 pickup, docking, and safety in host-side modules and macros. Finished Filament control Integrate AFC standalone for toolchanger filament mapping, loading, and runout handling. Finished ACE Pro Use an ACE Pro as another filament system, each slot feeding its own head, with auto feed and auto load. Finished ACE Pro multiplexing Feed several ACE slots into one head and swap between them. Planned Web and touchscreen Allow for switching filaments on the web. Partial Raspberry Pi host Use USB gadget mode to tunnel Klipper communication from a Raspberry Pi running the Klipper host to the printer. Testing Extend stock features Better VFA testing, stallguard and other similar improvements to software Partial

To see more features that are directly implemented in detail look at CFW Features.

These are goals, and not all of them are finished. The ACE Pro works with auto feed and auto load, multiplexing is in the planning stages, and the Raspberry Pi tunnel is in testing (see OpenCreator for SBC).

Gadget mode Klipper / RPI Klipper is very close to what AnyCubic's modding scene calls Tunneled Vanilla Klipper and a lot of initial inspiration was taken to go this route over direct MCU soldering, as it may not be possible on this board, as there has been no direct way (yet) to solder and allow USB passthrough for the MCUs.

items.title: OpenCreator Legacy
items.text: OpenCreator Legacy improves the Creator 5 while retaining its mostly stock FlashForge software and control behavior. It is the path for adding selected modifications without replacing the printer's entire control stack.

items.title: Extend the stock experience
items.text:
Legacy starts with the printer's existing FlashForge software. The Creator-5-Mods repository contains the guides and research, including root access, Loop Script, and Mainsail. The companion Creator-5-Scripts repository contains scripts intended to run on a rooted printer.

Legacy deprecation of support

Legacy no longer gets meaningful updates and will not get Discord support anymore, as CFW has been deemed stable enough to work on most printers. The legacy method still works and will gain version updates to continue to support newer versions of the FlashForge OS kernel package.

Legacy area Approach Base software Keep the printer's mostly stock FlashForge software and control behavior. (Preserving firmwareExe) Setup Follow individual guides and install only the modifications you want. Root access and scripts Use the documented root and Loop Script paths for printer-side tweaks. Toolchanging Continue using the factory workflow, with any compatible modifications from the guides. Web access Add tools such as Mainsail alongside the stock software. Updates and recovery Check each modification's prerequisite instructions before applying it.

For the newer and supported separate replacement stack, see OpenCreator CFW.

items.title: Plugins
items.text: OpenCreator CFW can install plugins: add-ons that bring their own Klipper modules, macros and Moonraker components without changing OpenCreator's own files. A plugin is a git repository with an opencreator-plugin.json manifest. The example plugin shows each part and is the place to start when making one.

items.title: Using plugins
items.text:
Plugins are managed with oc-plugin over SSH:

Command What it does oc-plugin search [word] The plugin catalog, or the entries matching a word. oc-plugin install <id or git URL> Download and enable a plugin, by its catalog id or from any git URL. --ref <branch or tag> picks a version. oc-plugin list Installed plugins, their version, whether they're enabled, and the git branch and commit. Plugins not made for this printer are marked. oc-plugin update [id] Pull the newest version of one plugin, or all of them. oc-plugin disable <id> / enable <id> Turn a plugin off or back on without removing it. oc-plugin remove <id> Uninstall it. --keep-data keeps its settings for a reinstall. oc-plugin status Each plugin's background programs: running or stopped, and their log file. oc-plugin logs <id> [item] The end of a plugin's logs. -n 200 for more lines, -f to keep following. oc-plugin start / stop / restart <id> [item] Start, stop or restart a plugin's background programs. oc-plugin sync Redo the links and includes; see How it works. oc-plugin moonraker [URL] Tunneled printers: show or set the SBC's Moonraker. --find looks for it, --scan lists every one and asks which. See Tunneled printers.

After a change, oc-plugin restarts Klipper and/or Moonraker itself, whichever the plugin needs. It never does that while the printer is printing or paused: it says so, and the change takes effect at the next restart. --no-restart skips the restart.

Plugins can say which printers and installs they're made for. install refuses one that isn't made for yours, and update keeps the old version if a new one isn't, or if its manifest is broken. --force installs it anyway. The SSH login banner shows how many plugins are installed.

items.title: Plugin catalog
items.text:
oc-plugin search lists the plugins in OpenCreator's catalog, split into official and unofficial ones, with where each one runs (SoC, SBC or both). Install one by its id, for example oc-plugin install hello.

Plugin Id Runs on Hello OpenCreator hello SoC, SBC Official. The example plugin: a Klippy module, a macro and a Moonraker endpoint. Printer Buddy Lite sep-ai SoC, SBC (tunneled) Official. Print failure detection on the printer's own X2600 RISC-V core, with a web page on port 7180. On a tunneled printer it's installed on the printer and finds the SBC's Moonraker by itself. Shake&Tune (numpy only) numpy-shaketune SoC Official, experimental. Klippain Shake&Tune on the printer itself, with a numpy-only stand-in for matplotlib. Needs a lot of system resources: each graph keeps the CPU busy for about a minute and uses up to about 130 MB of memory. Needs git (opkg install git). Graphs go to ShakeTune_results next to printer.cfg. OctoEverywhere for OpenCreator octoeverywhere SoC Unofficial. OctoEverywhere remote access and cameras. After installing, run sh /usr/data/opencreator/plugins/octoeverywhere/install.sh and follow its README. OpenCreator Display Manager display-manager SoC, SBC Unofficial. Switch between HelixScreen and GrumpyScreen with Klipper macros. Install Script Runner first. May slow the printer down; no support in SoC mode, including for slowdowns or MCU shutdowns. OpenCreator Spoolman Integration oc_spoolman_integration SoC, SBC Unofficial. A Spoolman spool per tool through AFC, so each tool books filament on its own spool. After installing, put your Spoolman server's address in oc-spoolman.conf (next to moonraker.conf), uncomment its [spoolman] section, then restart Moonraker and run FIRMWARE_RESTART. Orca Filament Profiles orca-filament-profiles SoC, SBC Unofficial. Pick which OrcaSlicer filament preset each AFC material uses when Orca syncs filaments (OrcaSlicer 2.5 or later). AFC now supports this itself, so this plugin may be of little use. If you still want it, put your mappings in orca-filament-profiles/mapping.cfg next to printer.cfg and restart Klipper. Samba Share samba-share SoC, SBC Unofficial. Shares /usr/data on the network over SMB. Needs Entware. The share is writable with guest access, so use it only on a trusted local network. Script Runner script-runner SoC, SBC Unofficial. Runs your own shell and Python scripts at startup, in SoC and tunneled mode, from /usr/data/opencreator/scripts/ (both/, soc/ or tunneled/). Needed by Touchscreen Server, so install it first. Touchscreen Server touchscreen-server SoC, SBC Unofficial. Remote access to the GrumpyScreen or HelixScreen touchscreen from a web browser. Install Script Runner first; after installing, open the URL shown in the install output. May slow the printer down, and it's only supported on tunneled printers. API Server api-server SoC, SBC Unofficial. HTTP API endpoints for Creator 5 mode switching and synchronization with a remote Linux host. Requires Script Runner on the Creator 5 and Mode Monitor on the Raspberry Pi, Radxa ZERO 3W or other compatible remote Linux host. Both components are required for complete mode switching and data synchronization. Auto light light-off-on-end SoC, SBC Unofficial. Turns the chamber light on when a print starts and off when it finishes; cancelling or an error leaves it on. Enabled by default and can be disabled with the auto_light toggle in Fluidd. OpenCreator Commander opencreator-commander SoC, SBC Unofficial. Filesystem manager with file browsing and editing, an integrated SSH terminal, customizable interface settings and read-only protection for critical system files. Supported only on tunneled printers. Use at your own risk.

Official plugins are made or checked by the OpenCreator team. Unofficial ones are listed so they're easy to find, but nobody from OpenCreator has reviewed them: read what a plugin does before installing it.

The catalog is catalog.json in opencreator-fs (fs/usr/data/opencreator/plugin-manager/). oc-plugin downloads it from GitHub each time, so a newly listed plugin shows up right away, without an OpenCreator update. Offline, it uses the last download (plugins/.catalog.json), or the copy that came with OpenCreator. To get a plugin listed, open a pull request adding it; the example plugin's README shows an entry.

Plugins installed from a git URL also show up in Fluidd and Mainsail's update manager as oc-plugin-<id>, so they can be updated from there like OpenCreator itself.

To see what's installed without SSH, run the OC_PLUGINS macro, or tap Plugins in GrumpyScreen's macros. It opens a dialog listing every plugin with its version, greyed out if it's disabled and red if its manifest is broken. Tap one for its description, author, what it adds to Klipper and Moonraker, and where it came from. oc-plugin sync rebuilds the list (as config/plugins/_oc-plugins.cfg) every time Klipper starts, so it stays current. Installing, updating and removing still happen over SSH.

To browse every plugin in the catalog, run OC_PLUGIN_MARKET, tap Plugin Marketplace in GrumpyScreen's macros, or tap Marketplace at the bottom of the OC_PLUGINS dialog. Official plugins are blue, unofficial ones yellow, installed ones grey and ones that don't run on this printer red. Tap one for its description, author, notes, link and the oc-plugin install command for it. The list comes from the catalog the printer last fetched: it's refreshed at every boot and whenever oc-plugin search, install or update runs, and Klipper shows the new list from its next start.

items.title: ZMOD plugins
items.text:
oc-plugin install also takes a plugin made for ZMOD, the AD5M/AD5X/C5(P) mod, for example oc-plugin install https://github.com/ghzserg/g28_tenz. Support is basic. A ZMOD plugin has no manifest, just a repo named after the plugin with <name>.cfg (or en/<name>.cfg if it's translated), so oc-plugin takes its id from the repo name and its version from git, and links only that config into Klipper. After that it's listed, updated, disabled and removed like any other plugin.

Its install.sh, uninstall.sh and update.sh are not run, because they expect ZMOD's folders, and Python modules have to be linked by hand, as on ZMOD itself. A plugin whose config uses ZMOD's own macros or settings won't work here as it is. Most plugins are expected to be rewritten.

Plugins run with full access

A plugin's Klipper and Moonraker code runs inside Klipper and Moonraker, with the same access to the printer as they have. Only install plugins you trust. An attacker could gain access to your network via a malicious plugin.

items.title: Making an OpenCreator plugin
items.text:
Copy the example plugin. Its README lists every manifest key. In short:

{
  "id": "hello",
  "name": "Hello OpenCreator",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "klippy_extras": ["klippy/oc_hello.py"],
  "klipper_config": "config/hello.cfg",
  "moonraker_components": ["moonraker/oc_hello.py"],
  "moonraker_config": "moonraker/hello.conf"
}
  • klippy_extras: Klippy modules, the same as a file in klippy/extras. A module is loaded by the config section of the same name, so oc_hello.py is loaded by [oc_hello].
  • klipper_config: one Klipper config file, with your module's section and macros. It's included after the rest of printer.cfg, so it can add to OpenCreator's sections.
  • moonraker_components and moonraker_config: the same, for Moonraker.

Module names must be unique. A plugin whose module has the same name as one of Kalico's, or as another plugin's, is refused and isn't installed. Give yours a prefix.

items.title: Startup items and scripts
items.text:
A plugin can also run its own programs:

"startup": [{ "name": "server", "exec": "bin/server.sh", "type": "service" }],
"scripts": { "install": "bin/install.sh", "update": "bin/install.sh", "uninstall": "bin/uninstall.sh" }
  • startup: programs started when the plugin is installed or enabled and at every boot, and stopped when it's disabled or removed. A service is started again if it exits (5 s later, backing off to a minute while it keeps failing). A once item runs at boot and stops. args and delay (up to 600 s) are optional.
  • scripts: install runs before anything is linked, and the plugin isn't installed if it fails. update runs after oc-plugin update pulls a new version, and uninstall before oc-plugin remove. Each gets up to 15 minutes.

Both run in the plugin folder with OC_PLUGIN_ID, OC_PLUGIN_DIR, OC_PLUGIN_DATA, OC_CONFIG_DIR, OC_KLIPPER_DIR and OC_MOONRAKER_URL set. OC_PLUGIN_DATA is a folder for the plugin's own files, and it's kept across updates. Startup items log to /tmp/oc-plugin-<id>-<name>.log, which oc-plugin logs shows. On the printer, /tmp is in RAM, so a log is moved aside to .log.1 once it passes 512 KB.

items.title: Compatibility
items.text:
"requires": { "models": ["Creator5Pro"], "modes": ["soc"] }
  • models: Creator5 and/or Creator5Pro, for hardware only one of them has, like the Pro's chamber heater. The model comes from the stock boot script, or from printer.model.cfg on SBC installs. If it can't be told, oc-plugin only warns.
  • modes: soc (Klipper on the printer itself) and/or sbc (Klipper on a Raspberry Pi or other SBC, including a printer tunneled to one).

Leave requires out if the plugin runs everywhere.

To try a plugin while writing it, install the folder straight from disk: oc-plugin install /usr/data/my-plugin. That's a copy, so install it again after each change, and it isn't offered in the update manager.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
Plugins are kept in /usr/data/opencreator/plugins/<id> (a git checkout). Nothing from a plugin is copied into Kalico or Moonraker. oc-plugin sync links it in:

Plugin part Where it goes klippy_extras Symlinked into Kalico's klippy/plugins/ (Klipper without that folder: klippy/extras/) klipper_config Symlinked as plugins/<id>.cfg next to printer.cfg, which includes [include plugins/*.cfg] moonraker_components Symlinked into Moonraker's moonraker/components/ moonraker_config Copied, with the plugin's [update_manager] section, to plugins/moonraker/<id>.conf, included by moonraker.conf with [include plugins/moonraker/*.conf]

Kalico's klippy/plugins/ is git-ignored, so Kalico updates leave plugin links alone. Kalico also refuses to start if a module there has the name of one of its own.

oc-plugin only removes or replaces links that point into the plugins folder. A file it didn't make is never touched. If something is in its way, it reports that and the plugin isn't installed. The two include lines are added to printer.cfg and moonraker.conf once, if they're missing. In printer.cfg the line goes before the SAVE_CONFIG block. plugins/moonraker/00-oc-plugins.conf only holds a comment. It's there because Moonraker, unlike Klipper, refuses an include that matches no files.

On the printer, 10-klipper.sh runs oc-plugin sync --only klipper before every Klippy start, and 20-msmr.sh runs oc-plugin sync --only moonraker before every Moonraker start. This is why an update from Fluidd, which only does a git pull and restarts, still links any file the new version added. oc-plugin itself lives in /usr/data/opencreator/plugin-manager/, which the installer and the OpenCreator updater keep up to date. 10-klipper.sh links it into /opt/bin.

items.title: Tunneled printers
items.text:
A tunneled printer counts as an SBC install, so it takes plugins made for sbc. oc-plugin runs on the printer as usual, and tunneled.sh starts the plugins' startup items at boot. Klipper and Moonraker are on the SBC, so a plugin's Klipper and Moonraker parts aren't linked on the printer, and nothing is restarted. Startup items and scripts get OC_TUNNELED=1.

Plugins that talk to Moonraker get the SBC's as OC_MOONRAKER_URL. oc-plugin moonraker --find finds it: it keeps the saved address if it still answers, and otherwise tries port 7125 on every address in the printer's own networks (neighbours it already knows first). It only accepts an OpenCreator tunnel SBC, one whose Moonraker has the opencreator-updater update entry or whose Klipper's MCUs are on /dev/ttyGS*. With several tunneled printers on one network it lists them all with their hostnames. Over SSH it asks which one is this printer's; run by a plugin it stops and says so. Pick one with oc-plugin moonraker --scan, or set it by hand with oc-plugin moonraker http://<sbc>:7125. The choice is saved in plugins/.moonraker-url.

items.title: Running oc-plugin on the SBC
items.text: oc-plugin also works on a Raspberry Pi running Klipper. There, the default folders are ~/opencreator-plugins, ~/klipper, ~/printer_data/config and ~/moonraker. Nothing runs sync at each start there, so run oc-plugin sync after updating a plugin from the update manager. To use other folders, set OC_PLUGINS_DIR, OC_KLIPPER_DIR, OC_CONFIG_DIR and OC_MOONRAKER_DIR, plus OC_MOONRAKER_URL for the restarts.

items.title: Current print workflow
items.text:
The C5_PRINT_START macro prepares only the tools the job uses. This page describes the current config; not every printer and filament combination has been tested.

The slicer or print dispatcher supplies TOOL=0..3, HOTEND, and BED. TOOLS=0,3, for example, identifies all tools used by a multi-tool job; TOOL must be in that list. HOTEND0 through HOTEND3 can override the shared hotend temperature for individual tools. The macro checks the physical filament-presence input for each used tool. A missing tool's filament cancels the job; unused tools are not required to be loaded.

When a file has no C5_PRINT_START line, the print dispatcher (virtual_sdcard.py) builds one from the first 64 KB and the last 64 KB of the file:

  • TOOL is the first T0–T3. If the file has none, it's the first slot with filament used.
  • HOTEND is the first M109, else the first M104. If neither exists, it's that tool's nozzle_temperature_initial_layer from Orca's config block. Orca leaves out the heating line in single-tool T0 jobs.
  • BED is the first M140 or M190.

If no hotend temperature can be found, the job stops before any motion, and the reason is printed to the console.

items.title: Preparation order
items.text:
flowchart TD
  A[Check filament in every used tool] -->|missing| X[Cancel the job]
  A --> C[Start preheating tools<br/>to max 100 °C & bed to temp]
  C --> B[Home, then wait for the bed]
  B --> D{Flow calibration<br/>or purge on?}
  D -->|yes| E[For each used tool:<br/>pick up, nozzle Z, heat,<br/>flow / purge, cool, dock]
  D -->|no| W
  E --> W[Wait for used tools<br/>to reach their preheat]
  W --> F{Bed leveling on?}
  F -->|yes| G[Adaptive mesh]
  F -->|no| H[Load saved mesh]
  G --> I[Pick up first tool, apply nozzle Z,<br/>park, other tools to idle temperature,<br/>wait for print temperature]
  H --> I
  I --> J{Purge on?}
  J -->|yes| M[KAMP purge line<br/>in front of the objects]
  J -->|no| O
  M --> O[Slicer G-code starts]
  1. Start a non-blocking preheat of every used tool to at most 100 °C, so the tools warm while the printer homes and the bed heats.
  2. Home for printing. If a tool is attached, the Creator 5 homing helper handles its docking before Z homing. Then wait for the bed to reach its target.
  3. If flow calibration or purge is enabled, prepare each used tool in turn: select it, establish its nozzle Z reference, heat it to its material temperature, run the selected flow and/or purge operation, cool it for docking, and release it.
  4. Wait for every used tool to reach its preheat (re-applied, since docking after priming may have left it cooler). Then clear the old mesh. When bed leveling is enabled, create an adaptive mesh. Otherwise, load the saved default mesh if one exists.
  5. Probe the bed center as a check, then select the job's initial tool. Apply its automatic nozzle Z, verify that a safe nozzle Z is available, smart park, and wait for its print temperature. The print's other tools are set to their slicer idle temperature (Orca's Idle temperature), or 100 °C if it has none.
  6. If purge is enabled, draw KAMP's purge line (LINE_PURGE) just in front of the printed objects. The slicer's print moves follow.

With purge_line_all_tools on, the print's other tools (TOOLS and the slicer's used tools) each draw a purge line too, after the mesh and before the initial tool is picked up. Each one is picked up, heated to its own first-layer temperature, draws its line further out than the last (purge_tool_spacing in KAMP_Settings.cfg, 8 mm by default), then cools and docks like after priming. The initial tool's line is drawn last, nearest the objects. A tool's line is left out, with a message, if there's no room for it in front of or left of the objects, or the file has no object outlines (Orca's Label objects).

The center probe check does not itself replace the automatic nozzle Z measurement. A missing safe nozzle Z is a print-stopping condition, not a reason to continue at zero offset.

Flow calibration, purge, the purge line and bed leveling can be toggled in the printer's Misc controls or overridden for a job with FLOW_CALIBRATION=0|1, PURGE=0|1, PURGE_LINE=0|1 and BED_LEVELING=0|1 (see How to toggle features). Turning off flow and purge removes those preparation operations; it does not bypass the filament-presence or nozzle-Z safety checks. See Printer features for how the flow measurement works.

At a normal job end, C5_PRINT_STOP handles tool parking and heater shutdown. The optional lower-bed-at-end setting is separate from print-start bed leveling. The printer configuration also routes cancellation through the stop sequence, but a shutdown can prevent ordinary G-code cleanup. Confirm the machine state before resuming after an MCU fault.

items.title: Notower (no prime tower)
items.text:
Warning

Notower needs a poop bucket fitted on the printer for the purged filament to drop into. A nozzle brush is recommended, so the purge doesn't trail back onto the print.

Notower purges into the bucket after each tool change instead of printing a prime tower. It only runs on prints that use more than one tool. Slice with the prime tower off, then turn it on for the print in either of these ways:

  • Tick Notower in OpenCreator Send and set the grams.
  • Add a line ; poop=0.05 to the G-code, for example in the slicer's start G-code. The number is grams per tool change; without one it's 0.05 g.

After every tool change in the print, the new tool goes to the bucket at 300 mm/s (20 000 mm/s² acceleration), heats to its print temperature, purges that much filament at 10 mm³/s, retracts 1 mm, moves 5 mm straight out of the bucket along X so it doesn't clip a docked toolhead, and goes back to the print. The weight becomes a length with the filament density from the slicer (PLA's 1.24 g/cm³ if it has none). 0.05 g of PLA, the default, takes about 4 s per tool change.

The tool changes during print start (priming, purge lines, picking up the first tool) don't purge, nor does a tool change by hand while paused. The bucket is on the frame, so the print position isn't lost, and the bed is never raised for it.

items.text: Printable parts made for the Creator 5 and 5 Pro from the community of the OpenCreator project.

items.title: Leveling tool
items.text:
OpenCreator FlashForge Creator 5 Leveling Tool on Printables.

A tool for leveling the bed. Use it with C5_SCREWS_TILT, which probes the bed screws and tells you how far to turn each one. Made by @SycoAniliz.

items.title: Want to list your own?
items.text: Let us know on our Discord!

items.title: First-time setup
items.text:
The first time you open Fluidd (or Mainsail, or look at the touchscreen) after installing OpenCreator, a dialog welcomes you and asks four questions:

  • Pressure advance calibration: measure each tool's pressure advance over the purge bucket at the start of every print.
  • Purging: purge each tool into the bucket at the start of every print.
  • Clog Detection: pause the print when a tool's filament wheel stops turning while filament is still loaded in it. Off by default.
  • Bed heat soak: before a fresh bed mesh, wait a few minutes at bed temperature so the plate finishes warping first. Off by default.

Then it says where your tool offsets and dock positions come from and how to recalibrate them, and recommends recalibrating VFA compensation once.

There's nothing you have to calibrate first: a first install on the printer (SoC) takes your printer's own calibration from FlashForge's config (/usr/data/config/printer.cfg), so it starts with the input shaper and the PID tuning of all four hotends and the bed that FlashForge measured. The bed mesh isn't taken; OpenCreator measures its own. A reinstall or update keeps the config you already have. Tunneled installs start with the template's values, so calibrate those yourself.

To calibrate yourself anyway: CALIBRATE_INPUT_SHAPER (or CALIBRATE_INPUT_SHAPER_GRAPH for graphs too), VFA_COMPENSATION, and C5_PID_CALIBRATE TOOL=1 TARGET=250 for a heater (add TOLERANCE=0.1 if a noisy heater won't settle; the default is 0.05).

One calibration we do recommend running once, when you're ready: VFA compensation. OpenCreator's VFA calibration is much better than stock's, and the dialog has a page saying so.

The next page explains when to run the two other calibrations: C5_CALIBRATE_OFFSETS if the tools' offsets weren't right on the stock firmware either, and C5_CALIBRATE_TOOL_POSITION if a tool doesn't dock or pick up cleanly.

Fluidd also starts with the OpenCreator macro layout: the macros grouped into On / Off, Calibrations, Toolhead and Misc. A layout you already set up in Fluidd is kept.

If you close the dialog before finishing, it comes back within a minute. Once you reach the last page it won't appear again. Both choices are ordinary switches under Fans & Outputs, so you can change them at any time. To go through the dialog again, send C5_FIRST_SETUP in the console.

items.title: Camera streamer (experimental option)
items.text:
The camera streams with mjpg_streamer by default. ustreamer is available as an experimental alternative. It passes the camera's own MJPEG frames through with almost no CPU, copes better with several viewers or a slow connection, and skips repeated frames when nothing moves.

To switch, edit camera.conf in the config folder (Fluidd or Mainsail: Configuration), then restart the printer:

streamer: ustreamer

Switching to ustreamer needs an internet connection, over Wi-Fi or wired Ethernet: the printer downloads it the first time.

streamer: mjpg_streamer switches back. The camera keeps the same port, addresses and colour settings, so Fluidd, Mainsail and Timelapse need no changes. If ustreamer stops three times in a row within 30 seconds of starting, the printer goes back to mjpg_streamer until the next restart, and says so in /tmp/opencreator.log. ustreamer's own log is /usr/data/logs/ustreamer.log.

items.title: Screen timeout
items.text:
The touchscreen's backlight turns off after 5 minutes without a touch, and on again at the next touch. That waking touch doesn't press anything. A keyboard or gamepad on the printer's USB keeps it on too, and so does Sonic Mania or DOOM while you play.

To change the time, edit screen-timeout.conf in the config folder from Fluidd or Mainsail: timeout: 300 is in seconds, and 0 keeps the screen on. The change takes effect within a few seconds.

It runs as its own small service beside the screen app, so it works with GrumpyScreen and HelixScreen alike.

items.title: Timelapse
items.text:
The OpenCreator Installer sets up Moonraker Timelapse. It takes a camera frame at every layer change and renders them into an MP4 when the print finishes. The videos show up under Timelapse in Fluidd and Mainsail, where you can also change its settings (frame rate, parking the toolhead for each frame, and so on).

To record a print, add TIMELAPSE_TAKE_FRAME to the slicer's layer change G-code (see Slicer Configuration). Without it, only hyperlapse mode records, which takes frames at a fixed interval instead.

Printer (SoC) Raspberry Pi (tunnel) Camera The printer camera, through its snapshot URL The webcam you set up in Fluidd or Mainsail ffmpeg FlashForge's own build, already on the printer Installed from apt Frames /usr/data/opencreator/timelapse/frames/ /tmp/timelapse/ Videos /usr/data/opencreator/timelapse/ ~/printer_data/timelapse/

Rendering on the printer

On the printer, ffmpeg runs at the lowest priority so it never holds up Klipper, which makes rendering slow: expect a few minutes for a long print. Frames are kept on storage rather than in /tmp, which is RAM and too small for a long print.

Moonraker's update manager keeps Timelapse current, as the timelapse entry.

items.title: Input shaper graphs
items.text:
CALIBRATE_INPUT_SHAPER_GRAPH does the same as CALIBRATE_INPUT_SHAPER (measures both axes, applies the recommended shaper and saves it; add SAVE=0 to save later), and also draws a graph of each axis on the printer, the same graph Klipper's calibrate_shaper.py makes on a PC. It is under Calibrations on Fluidd's Macros card (Uncategorized on installs whose macro layout is older than the macro).

The graphs are saved to the config folder as input_shaper/shaper_x.png and input_shaper/shaper_y.png; open them from the config files in Fluidd or Mainsail.

  • Left axis: the measured vibrations (X, Y, Z and their sum) at each frequency. Peaks are resonances; After shaper is what the recommended shaper leaves of them.
  • Right axis: how much each shaper lets through at each frequency. The recommended shaper is dash-dotted; the legend gives each one's frequency, remaining vibrations, smoothing and the highest acceleration it suits.

The figures come from Kalico's own shaper code, so they match what SHAPER_CALIBRATE reports in the console.

items.title: Flow Calibration in the Creator 5 factory firmware
items.text:
The touchscreen calls this Flow Calibration, but the routine is intended to test pressure advance. It does not measure a printed line's width, weigh extruded plastic, or calculate an extrusion multiplier. The host tries several pressure-advance values while the eboard observes the extruder motor driver's SG_RESULT load signal. The eboard reports whether each sampled waveform passes its check.

The sequence below is reconstructed from the factory firmwareExe.i64 database, principally BuildPage::clearNozzlePrint and CommMgr::paTestMgr, and from the factory eBoard.hex.

items.title: The stock test, step by step
items.text:
1. The host resets the extruder position with G92 E0, switches to relative extrusion with M83, sets acceleration to 5000 mm/s² and square-corner velocity to 9 mm/s, enables the X/Y motor-driver control pins, and waits for queued motion to finish.
  2. It tries these pressure-advance candidates in this order: 0.0100, 0.0200, 0.0150, 0.0350, 0.0250, 0.0300, and 0.0400. For each candidate it sends PA_ACTION ACTION=11 PC=666 to arm the eboard measurement, then SET_PRESSURE_ADVANCE ADVANCE=<candidate>.
  3. The carriage starts each candidate at X40 and a Y position from 50 to 80 in 5 mm steps. It extrudes across six X strokes ending at X60, X100, X120, X140, X180, and X200. The X and Y movements don't actually happen and get discarded, this is mostly to trick Klippy into thinking PA can be used. The short strokes extrude 1.13573 mm of filament at F1080 (18 mm/s); the long strokes extrude 2.27146 mm at F10980 (183 mm/s). Alternating slow and fast motion creates the motor-load transient that the eboard examines.
  4. The host sends PA_ACTION ACTION=0 PC=666, waits with M400, and reads PA_GET. It treats a returned value of 9 as a pass for that candidate.

The eboard firmware's pa_action handler resets its result and sample area when action 11 starts a measurement, switches its acquisition mode, then finalizes the capture when action 0 arrives. get_emcu_pa_value reports the result back to the host as pa_value value=<number>. 9 means "pass"; it isn't the measured pressure advance. How the eboard decides is described below. The host always sends PC=666, and what that value means isn't known yet.

items.title: Where the waveform comes from
items.text:
The host does not synthesize an electrical waveform. It commands a sequence of extruder moves. Changing extrusion speed changes the motor's mechanical load; the TMC2209 turns that load into successive SG_RESULT register values. The eboard reads those values over UART and stores valid replies in time order. Plotting sample index against SG_RESULT produces the waveform that the classifier examines. Consecutive samples are roughly 2 ms apart when no reply is lost; dropped replies make sample index an imperfect time axis. It is a driver load estimate, not a direct motor current measurement or a measurement of deposited plastic.

In the current OpenCreator/Kalico bucket test, the carriage stays at the purge bucket while E alone runs through six relative extrusion moves:

Segment Filament commanded Default E speed Nominal time at speed Slow 1.13573 mm 4.5 mm/s 252 ms Fast 2.27146 mm 22.875 mm/s 99 ms Slow 1.13573 mm 4.5 mm/s 252 ms Slow 1.13573 mm 4.5 mm/s 252 ms Fast 2.27146 mm 22.875 mm/s 99 ms Slow 1.13573 mm 4.5 mm/s 252 ms

Those durations are distance divided by speed, not exact captured pulse widths: acceleration, motion planning, and transitions between moves alter the actual timing. The test commands 9.08584 mm of filament per candidate. PA_ACTION ACTION=11 starts sampling before the moves; M400 drains them, and PA_ACTION ACTION=0 closes the capture. The eboard polls the driver about every 2 ms, accepts only complete replies with a valid CRC, and reserves 2,000 sample slots (about four seconds). Missing or invalid replies are not valid load observations.

Current limitation: Kalico's extruder planner applies pressure advance only when an extrusion move also has X or Y travel. These bucket strokes are E-only, so changing SET_PRESSURE_ADVANCE between candidates does not itself reshape their E motion. A pass currently shows that the driver-load waveform matches the eboard's stroke criteria; it does not prove that the selected pressure-advance value is optimal. The factory routine issues XY/E strokes, whereas the current bucket-safe port intentionally omits XY movement. The stock firmware's full waveform and its PA discrimination have not been established by this Kalico implementation alone.

items.title: How the eboard judges a stroke
items.text:
This is how OpenCreator's own eboard firmware (in Kalico, src/c5_eboard_pa.c) does it.

Sampling. While a measurement runs, the eboard asks the extruder's TMC2209 driver for its load reading (SG_RESULT) about every 2 ms, roughly 500 times a second. The response parser checks its framing and CRC before storing a reading.

Judging. In those readings the eboard looks for a stroke:

  1. Start: the reading climbs by more than 99 without dropping.
  2. End: the reading stays at 70 or below for 0.4 s (or the readings run out).
  3. Plateau: the part above 150, minus 60 ms at each end.

The stroke passes when all of these are true:

  • The plateau averages more than 150.
  • The plateau lasts about 160–300 ms, roughly one slow stroke.
  • Early in the stroke the reading jumps more than 20% above the plateau, for at least 3 readings.
  • At the end it drops cleanly, from between half and all of the plateau level down to near zero.

If any stroke passes, the eboard answers 9.

items.title: What can make it fail
items.text:
• Klipper talking to the same driver. Klipper checks the extruder driver about once a second over the same wire, which garbles the eboard's readings and stops the test from ever passing. OpenCreator's flow test now pauses those checks while it runs.
  • No X/Y motion. Klipper only applies pressure advance to moves that include X or Y motion, so extruding in place tests nothing. Like the stock firmware, OpenCreator runs the stock X/Y strokes, but with the X/Y motors held still: they stay powered and locked, they just aren't sent any steps. The nozzle stays over the bucket, and afterwards the printer knows exactly where it is again, so no re-homing is needed.
  • Driver mode. The TMC2209 only gives a useful SG_RESULT in its quiet StealthChop mode, so OpenCreator runs the extruder driver in StealthChop (stealthchop_threshold: 999999 on [tmc2209 extruder] to [tmc2209 extruder3]). Klipper's default would be SpreadCycle. On stock firmware the eboard sets up the driver itself, so the stock config has no driver settings to compare with.

To see the driver settings the stock eboard uses, run DUMP_TMC STEPPER=extruder in the console of a printer still on stock firmware.

items.title: How it chooses and applies a result
items.text:
One pass tests up to seven candidates and keeps the smallest candidate for which the eboard returned 9. The host allows up to five passes, stopping once three passes produce a valid candidate. It averages those three selected values to produce that tool's result. If fewer than three passes succeed, the test reports failure rather than producing a new value. The routine also cleans up its motor-driver test mode after completion or interruption.

After preparing the tools, the print-start code sends SET_PA_ADVANCE with the successful T0–T3 results and ENABLE=1. Entries without a result are filled with 99.0 as placeholders. If flow testing is off, or no valid tool result is available, it sends SET_PA_ADVANCE T0=99.0 T1=99.0 T2=99.0 T3=99.0 ENABLE=0. These final per-tool settings are distinct from the temporary SET_PRESSURE_ADVANCE candidate applied during each test.

items.title: Host pressure-advance test (OpenCreator, experimental)
items.text:
C5_FLOW_STROKES METHOD=host is OpenCreator's own pressure-advance test. The stock test only says whether each fixed candidate passes or fails. This one has Klippy look at every driver reading itself and work out the pressure advance, so it isn't limited to the stock candidates. It takes about a minute per tool, where the stock test takes about two and a half.

It needs OpenCreator's eboard firmware with the reading stream (flashed by installer 0.4.8 and later), and StealthChop on the extruder drivers, the same as the stock test.

At print start it runs when the host_pressure_advance switch is on (Fans & Outputs, C5_MISC_HOST_PRESSURE_ADVANCE_ON/_OFF, or HOST_PRESSURE_ADVANCE=1 on C5_PRINT_START), with APPLY=1. It is off by default and separate from the stock flow_calibration switch. With both on, the stock test runs first and the host test after it; if the host result is rejected, the stock value stays.

items.title: The idea
items.text:
Pressure advance models nozzle pressure as trailing the extruder motor. The right advance is the one that cancels that lag: by the time the motor reaches a steady speed, pressure has already caught up.

So the test runs the extruder fast at a constant speed and watches the motor's load (SG_RESULT) during that steady part:

  • Too little advance: pressure is still building, so the load keeps rising.
  • Too much advance: the extra push overshoots, so the load falls back.
  • Right advance: the load stays flat.

Because the motor speed isn't changing during that part, a change in load can only come from the melt pressure. The test measures this drift at a few advance values and finds where it crosses zero.

items.title: Readings
items.text:
The stock eboard firmware only keeps its readings to make its own pass/fail decision. OpenCreator's eboard firmware also keeps each reading with the eboard's clock time, and Klippy downloads them afterwards (get_pa_stream). That's about 500 readings a second, up to 6,000 (12 s) per run. Each one is matched to the extruder's commanded position and speed at that moment.

Without that firmware, SENSOR=sg has Klippy poll the driver itself instead, which gives far fewer readings.

items.title: The strokes
items.text: Each run starts with 0.4 s at 1 mm/s of filament, then six strokes. Each stroke is 0.5 s at 10.4 mm/s, then 0.4 s back at 1 mm/s. As in the stock test, the X/Y motors are held still, and each move has X/Y travel four times its extrusion so Klipper applies pressure advance to it. The first stroke is only a warm-up and isn't scored.

items.title: Scoring a stroke
items.text:
Every stroke is measured from the moment it reaches speed:

  • Early: 0.03–0.09 s in, just after the advance's own push has finished.
  • Late: the rest of the stroke, up to 0.02 s before it ends.

The stroke's drift is (early − late) / late.

The motor's load reading also ripples with each electrical cycle of the motor: once every four full steps, which is 0.0589 mm of filament on these extruders. That ripple was more than half of the reading noise during a stroke. The test fits it across all of a run's strokes (four harmonics) and removes it before it compares early and late.

items.title: Finding the answer
items.text:
1. The test runs at advances of 0, 0.05 and 0.10, which gives 15 scored strokes.
  2. It fits a straight line through (advance, drift) and takes the advance where the line crosses zero. A stroke whose reading drops to 0 or near it stalled the motor and isn't used.
  3. Now and then a stroke reads far off. Up to a tenth of the strokes that sit more than four robust standard deviations off the line are dropped, and the line is fitted again.
  4. If the load barely responds (|t| below 4), the test runs the same advances again, up to 24 runs in all. PLA needs this: its pressure settles within about 20 ms, so each stroke shows only a small drift.
  5. The fit gives a 95% range for the answer. If that range is wider than 0.03, the test runs twice more, at the answer ±0.01. It repeats this until the range is narrow enough, or until it has used six runs on this, the same as a normal nine-run test.

The answer is rejected, and nothing is changed, when:

Reason Meaning Load does not respond The drift barely changes with advance (|t| below 4). Usually the driver isn't in StealthChop. Drifts the wrong way Drift rises with advance, the opposite of what pressure does. Outside the tested range The answer is more than 0.02 outside the advances that were tested. Too uncertain The 95% range is still wider than 0.03 after nine runs.

The trace is written to /tmp/c5_flow_T<tool>.csv (one row per reading: run, advance, time, filament position, reading, commanded speed and acceleration). The console shows each stroke's drift and the result, for example:

T2 host flow test: pressure advance 0.0751 (95%: 0.0633-0.0869, t=-6.3, 25 strokes, 5 runs)

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Parameter Default APPLY 0 1 sets the result as the tool's pressure advance if it isn't rejected ADVANCES 0,0.05,0.10 Advances for the first runs, comma separated REFINE 1 0 skips the extra runs MAX_RUNS 9 Limit on runs, including the extra ones WEAK_RUNS 24 Limit on runs when the load barely responds; 0 turns the repeats off CURRENT 1 Experimental: extruder run current during the strokes, as a fraction of the configured one. Lower makes pressure show up more, but noise grows as fast. Below about 0.8 the advance's push stalls the motor: on PETG this left too few strokes at PA 0.10 and gave 0.058 instead of about 0.075. SENSOR eboard eboard: the eboard's reading stream; sg: Klippy polls the driver (used when the eboard firmware has no stream) FAST 10.4 Stroke speed, mm/s of filament SLOW 1 Speed between strokes, mm/s of filament STROKES 6 Strokes per run FAST_TIME 0.5 Stroke length, s SLOW_TIME 0.4 Time between strokes, s LEAD 0.4 Slow time before the first stroke, s RATIO 0.25 Filament per mm of the (held) X/Y travel

The tool must be attached and at printing temperature, with Z calibrated, as for the stock test.

items.title: Results so far
items.text:
On T2 with PETG at 255 °C, five runs gave 0.067, 0.068, 0.074, 0.075 and 0.079 (one of these was rejected as too uncertain, before the extra runs were added). The others took under a minute each. The stock test gives 0.028–0.030 for the same filament.

The stock test is limited by the motion more than by the filament. Its end check fails above about 0.037 because the retract outruns the stroke's own speed, and its spike check needs at least about 0.02. That leaves about 0.03 for most filaments.

Neither number has been checked against a print yet, so leave APPLY at 0 until it has. To check, print a pressure-advance tower with the same filament:

TUNING_TOWER COMMAND=SET_PRESSURE_ADVANCE PARAMETER=ADVANCE START=0 FACTOR=.005

Then compare the height where the corners look best with both results.

items.title: Filament dryer (VDS)
items.text:
On the SoC install, OpenCreator drives FlashForge's two-chamber VDS filament dryer the same way the stock firmware does: over the printer's internal serial port /dev/ttyS3 at 115200 baud. Plug the dryer in where FlashForge says to before installing: the installer only turns the dryer controls on when a dryer answers. It then writes printer.accessory.dryer.cfg, which loads printer.dryer.cfg. If you add a dryer later, rerun the installer or add [include printer.dryer.cfg] to printer.cfg yourself.

Command What it does C5_DRYER_START CHAMBER=A\|B\|AB TEMP=45-85 HOURS=1-48 Dry one or both chambers (MINUTES=60-2880 works instead of HOURS) C5_DRYER_STOP CHAMBER=A\|B\|AB Stop drying C5_DRYER_PAUSE CHAMBER=A\|B\|AB Turn the heaters off; start again with C5_DRYER_START C5_DRYER_DEHUMIDIFY CHAMBER=A\|B\|AB ENABLE=0\|1 Keep a chamber dry after drying C5_DRYER_STATUS Firmware version, and each chamber's state, temperature, humidity and time left C5_DRYER_PLA, C5_DRYER_PETG, C5_DRYER_ABS, C5_DRYER_OFF Presets (50, 65 and 80 °C for 6 hours) and stop; add CHAMBER=A or B for one chamber

CHAMBER defaults to both. The chambers also show up as the temperature sensors dryer_a and dryer_b, with their humidity, so Fluidd and Mainsail graph them. Macros can read printer.creator5_dryer (connected, firmware_version, and per chamber drying, temperature, humidity, remaining_minutes).

The dryer's own firmware limits drying to 45-85 °C and 1-48 hours. OpenCreator doesn't update the dryer's firmware; if C5_DRYER_STATUS says it is in its bootloader, update it from stock FlashForge firmware.

items.title: Offset Calibration
items.text:
Offset calibration aligns the nozzles of T0–T3 for printing. It is separate from locating their docks. The Creator 5 port exposes it through C5_CALIBRATE_OFFSETS; measurements and the levelboard reference are kept in /usr/data/firmwareRes/config/extruder.json.

Calibration cannot run during a print. If a tool is attached, the carriage first raises it to the safe Z clearance and docks it. The ordinary calibration pin is then probed at two known locations. Their contact-height difference is used to reject a plate that may still be installed and to set a safe approach floor for the following measurements.

With the carriage bare, the routine contacts the levelboard fixture to establish its Z reference, then scans outward from its center for the X+, Y+, X-, and Y- edges. Each edge scan is limited to 7 mm; opposite edges give the fixture's X/Y center. The routine then picks up T0, probes its Z against the fixture, scans its four X/Y edges, raises clear of the fixture, and docks it. It repeats that sequence for T1, T2, and T3. The saved X/Y printing offsets are each tool's measured center relative to T0. Its nozzle Z offset uses the tool's measured Z relative to the fixture reference, plus the separate per-tool Z fine adjustment. The code rejects measurements beyond its configured correction limits or an unsafe resulting nozzle Z offset.

CFW

The all-tool run saves only after all four tools succeed. It makes a backup of extruder.json and replaces that file atomically, so a failed tool does not leave a partially saved set. The measured offsets are also applied to the active tool through Klipper's G-code offset when it is selected.

A single tool can be recalibrated with TOOL=0 through TOOL=3. It still requires removing and checking the build plate; it docks any attached tool, checks the ordinary pin, and automatically picks up the requested tool. LEVELBOARD=0 skips refreshing the bare fixture reference for a single tool, but does not skip that tool's levelboard measurement. Z=0 performs XY-only calibration and needs a configured scan height or SCAN_Z; the default Z=1 probes the nozzle Z automatically. TOOL=ALL always refreshes the fixture reference and requires Z=1.

items.title: Baby stepping
items.text:
Baby stepping a tool's Z offset during a print, from Fluidd's or Mainsail's Z adjust buttons or SET_GCODE_OFFSET Z_ADJUST=, is saved as you go. It's saved as that tool's Z adjustment in /usr/data/firmwareRes/config/zoffset.json, the same value the touchscreen's Z offset sets. Each nozzle keeps its own value: a step goes to whichever head is attached. The next print, and the same nozzle after a toolchange, start from it, read from that file each time, so it's kept across restarts too.

Macro What it does LIST_BABYSTEP Shows the saved Z adjustment for every tool. TOOL=2 shows only T2. CLEAR_BABYSTEP TOOL=1 Resets T1's saved Z adjustment to 0. With no TOOL, or TOOL=ALL, it resets all four.

Clearing the attached tool also takes the adjustment off its current Z offset. Because the touchscreen uses the same value, clearing a tool also clears its touchscreen Z offset.

A Z change of more than 1 mm at once isn't treated as baby stepping and isn't saved. To stop saving baby stepping, add persist_babystep: False to [creator5_toolchanger].

items.title: Toolhead Dock Calibration
items.text:
Toolhead dock calibration, called Extruder Position Calibrate in the factory UI, finds the physical pickup/docking X/Y coordinates for one tool. It does not change the nozzle offsets used to align layers during a print. In the Creator 5 port, run C5_CALIBRATE_TOOL_POSITION T=0 through T=3, or use the underlying EXTRUDER_POSITION_CALIBRATE T=n command.

Before starting, park all four tools, home the printer, raise Z to at least the configured safe clearance (10 mm in the supplied config), and let every toolhead cool below 50 °C. A print must not be active. The build plate does not need to be removed for this calibration.

  1. The routine disables X/Y motors and asks you to move the bare master carriage by hand to the chosen parked tool. It waits for both that dock's holder sensor and its grab sensor to register contact.
  2. Once contact is detected, it asks you to release the carriage and waits briefly before taking over. It latches the tool and pulls it clear, checking that the holder sensor released while the grab sensor remains active.
  3. It measures X and Y against the printer's X/Y home references, calculates the dock coordinates, and rejects a correction beyond the configured limit (2 mm in the supplied config).
  4. It rehomes X/Y, redocks the tool using the measured coordinates, and only then saves them as x_check_pos/y_check_pos for T0, or the corresponding numbered keys for T1–T3, in extruder.json. A timestamped backup is made first.

If contact, sensor verification, measurement, or redocking fails, the routine does not save new dock coordinates.

items.title: Mainboard and power supply fans
items.text:
The mainboard has two fans of its own: one cooling the board and the X/Y/Z motor drivers, and one in the power supply. Stock runs both at full speed whenever the motors are powered or a hotend is heating. OpenCreator only runs them as fast as the printer needs, so they are much quieter most of the time.

  • Mainboard fan: follows the mainboard chip's own temperature. Off below 54.5 °C, from 30% at 54.5 °C up to full speed at 65 °C, and at least 40% while the motors are powered, for the drivers.
  • Power supply fan: follows the power supply's estimated load, from the hotends' heater power and the motors. 30% at light load, at least 50% while a hotend is heating, full speed at about 120 W. It never runs slower than the mainboard fan. Once the load is gone it keeps running for a minute at most 80%, then stops.

Both ramp up and down smoothly instead of switching between off and full. They are checked every second on their own timer, so long commands such as PID calibration, heat-up waits or homing don't stop them.

During input shaper, VFA and ripple calibration both fans are held at 50%, so their vibration stays the same through the measurement.

C5_BOARD_FANS shows both speeds, the mainboard temperature and the estimated load. C5_BOARD_FANS HOLD=0.5 holds both fans at 50% (HOLD=-1 releases them), and any setting can be changed until the next restart, e.g. C5_BOARD_FANS MAX_TEMP=65. To keep a change, edit [c5_board_fans] in printer.base.cfg.

items.title: MCU temperatures
items.text: Fluidd and Mainsail show the temperature of the mainboard chip (mainboard_mcu) and of the toolhead board's chip (toolhead_mcu). They are only for keeping an eye on things; the mainboard one also drives the mainboard fan.

items.title: Motion guard
items.text: The motion guard watches the X, Y and Z motors for skipped steps and stalls during a print, from the mainboard's own motor control. It is off by default, as it reported too many false alarms while the motors were crawling or holding still. C5_MOTION_GUARD ENABLE=1 turns it on until the next restart (ACTION=pause to pause the print instead of warning), and C5_MOTION_STATUS shows what it has counted.

items.title: Wired Ethernet
items.text:
The Creator 5 only has Wi-Fi, and FlashForge's firmware has no drivers for USB network adapters. OpenCreator adds them, so a USB Ethernet adapter in the printer's USB port gives it a wired connection. Android USB tethering works the same way.

Adapter Examples Realtek RTL8152, RTL8153, RTL8156 Most USB Ethernet adapters, 100 Mbit to 2.5 Gbit ASIX AX88772 100 Mbit adapters ASIX AX88179, AX88178A Gigabit adapters Standard CDC ECM / NCM Adapters that use the generic USB network class RNDIS Android phones with USB tethering on

Plug the adapter in and connect it to your router; within about 10 seconds it gets an address by DHCP, like Wi-Fi does. It can be plugged in or out while the printer is on.

  • The cable is used while it's in. Wi-Fi stays connected, and if the cable is pulled out or loses its link, the printer goes back to Wi-Fi at once.
  • The adapter has its own IP address, different from the printer's Wi-Fi one. Find it in your router's list of devices, and use it in your browser and slicer.
  • SoC installs only. On a Raspberry Pi tunnel install the printer's USB port talks to the Pi, so this isn't used.
  • Kernel 2.0.7 or 2.0.8. The drivers were built and checked for FlashForge's kernel packages 2.0.7 and 2.0.8 only, and aren't loaded on others. Over SSH, ls /usr/prog/PROGRAM/kernel/ shows which one the printer has.

If the adapter isn't picked up, /usr/data/logs/usb-ethernet.log says why, and ip addr over SSH shows the adapter and its address.

items.title: SBC Installation and Configuration
items.text:
SBC / RPI Klipper for replacing the Mips32 Host that comes with the printer. The printer's own board keeps only a serial bridge that forwards its four MCUs to the SBC over one USB cable. Klipper, Moonraker and Fluidd run on the SBC.

    K[Kalico / Klipper] --- M[Moonraker] --- F[Fluidd]
  end
  subgraph P["Creator 5 SoC"]
    B[c5-tunnel bridge]
  end

  B --- HB[heaterBoard]
  B --- EB[eBoard]
